ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 153 ACME BRE Graph This graph shows as a function of time, the fuel flow (red) and three optical flame measurements from a test in which pure ethylene was burned. The optical flame measurements were made with Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) modules of OH* chemiluminescence (purple), CH* chemiluminescence (light blue), and broadband emissions in the visible and near UV spectrum (dark blue). OH* and CH* are transient molecules which, in the process of chemiluminescence, emit a photon at specific wavelengths when they drop to a lower energy level. The CH* chemiluminescence is the principal source of the blue seen in hydrocarbon flames, while OH* is in the ultraviolet and is used in ACME to indicate ignition and extinction. The initially sooty flame was ignited at 32 seconds, after which the hot-wire igniter was retracted. At about 60 seconds, after the ceramic fiber array was inserted, the flame became quasi-steady. But the PMT signals weakened with time, where the low-momentum flame became increasingly blanketed by carbon dioxide and water vapor in the absence of buoyancy. At about 95 seconds, the increasing radiative loss caused the flame’s top to

e, where the low-momentum flame became increasingly blanketed by carbon dioxide and water vapor in the absence of buoyancy. At about 95 seconds, the increasing radiative loss caused the flame’s top to quench, creating a hole in the flame. This hole allowed the fuel and oxygen, which are normally separated by the flame, to directly mix. This mixing enhanced flammability, and the flame quickly reestablished and closed the hole, but then again, it locally quenched. This oscillatory behavior happened repeatedly at roughly 1 Hz with the flame opening growing with time until the flame became just a ring. We saw this phenomenon in the first round of BRE testing performed on ISS in 2019. A paper about computational modeling of it is now in press. At about 135 seconds, the flame began to partially detach from the rim of the burner and then reattach until it completely extinguished at 148 seconds.

ACME/BRE Final Report (2022) 1 Feb. 2022 174 Appendix N. Summary of the ISS data collection The BRE data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were subsequently transported to the ground. The BRE image data includes images from the following cameras: 1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but those settings were consistent within each individual test) 2. CFI intensified camera, typically used with a CH* filter (and likely always or nearly always for BRE) 3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, and HiBMs cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software Interface Des

the analog video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). The raw data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 3 1. Overview The Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which the tests were conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Peter B. Sunderland of the Department of Fire Protection Engineering at the University of Maryland. The two Co-Investigators (Co-Is) are Profs. Richard L. Axelbaum and Forman A. Williams who are respectively from the Washington University of St. Louis and the University of California, San Diego (UCSD). Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is the Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including CFI-G and the rest of the ACME investigations. In ACME’s preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team included Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. The ISS operations for CFI-G were conducted

he Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team included Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. The ISS operations for CFI-G were conducted from March to Oct. 2021 in two sequential rounds of testing. The two rounds occurred during Increments 64-65 and 65-66 and respectively featured normal and inverse flames. The inverse flame tests were conducted with the chamber filled with a mixture of nitrogen and gaseous fuel while an oxygen/nitrogen mixture flowed from the burner. As a result, the inverse flames were effectively inside out, e.g., where the soot formed outside rather than inside of the flames. Although it was in the second round, the final day of CFI-G testing was carried out in the normal flame configuration, with gaseous fuel (with or without nitrogen) flowing into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere. This was an added test day carried out under conditions in which low-temperature combustion occurred during the first round of testing. CFI-G was a late addition to ACME, where the experiment was jointly selected for spaceflight by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space

f testing. CFI-G was a late addition to ACME, where the experiment was jointly selected for spaceflight by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS) rather than NASA. The selection was notably announced after the core ACME hardware had launched to the ISS and just weeks before ACME’s on-orbit operations began. It is effectively an extension of ACME’s Flame Design experiment for which the PI and Co-I are respectively Axelbaum and Sunderland. And it is likewise a follow-on to the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI), led by Williams, in which liquid droplets were burned rather than gaseous fuel. Although CFI-G wasn’t selected for spaceflight by NASA, its ISS operations and the development of its unique hardware, software, and procedure were carried out by the same teams of personnel as the other ACME experiments, primarily from ZIN Technologies, Inc.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 4 2. Science Overview A. Background This background is the Project Summary from the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. Overview: Cool diffusion flames were discovered in 2012 aboard the ISS. This spawned a rapidly growing research field, but only a small number of measurements at limited conditions are available. Consequently, cool flame kinetics mechanisms cannot be adequately tested or advanced. This could be impeding the development of cleaner and more efficient internal combustion engines. It is proposed here to observe cool diffusion flames supported by porous spherical burners fed with propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. Normal and inverse flames will be considered for a broad range of dilution conditions and pressures. The ISS is the ideal platform for observing cool diffusion flames because they typically require 20 s to establish and they could burn indefinitely. Tests will be performed using the ACME insert in the CIR. Minimal hardware development will be req

l diffusion flames because they typically require 20 s to establish and they could burn indefinitely. Tests will be performed using the ACME insert in the CIR. Minimal hardware development will be required because the spherical porous burners and gas delivery system will be those used by the Flame Design flight experiment, while the diagnostics will be those used by the CFI flight experiment. The objectives are to observe diverse cool diffusion flames aboard the ISS, to simulate the tests with an advanced CFD model, and to identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that accurately models these conditions. Intellectual Merit: Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The proposed experiments will take advantage of many state-of-the-art diagnostics that are already available on the ISS. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. An

tage of many state-of-the-art diagnostics that are already available on the ISS. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. An advanced CFD model will simulate the flames and will aid the testing and development of cool flame kinetics models. Observing cool flames burning as steady spherical diffusion flames will yield valuable insight into cool flame chemical kinetics. The measurements proposed cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. Broader Impacts: The research will be disseminated widely to the combustion research community and to industry. It should advance the state-of-the-art in cool flame kinetics mechanisms, which in turn could lead to cleaner, more efficient internal combustion engines. This project will have several educational impacts. Graduate students will conduct much of the

The PI will team with two organizations at UMD - the Women in Engineering Program and the Center for Minorities in Science and Engineering - to foster interest in science and engineering among female and minority secondary school students. A day-long flame laboratory will be developed for secondary school students that will foster their interest in combustion and scientific inquiry. B. Rationale for Microgravity This is the ‘Justification for Testing Aboard the ISS’ section (3.1) of the experiment’s 2017 proposal in response to a solicitation from the NSF/CASIS Collaboration on Combustion and Thermal Transport Processes Research on the International Space Station to Benefit Life on Earth. The included equation is formatted differently in this copy. Previous ground-based microgravity experiments have demonstrated the scientific value of spherical, burner-supported diffusion flames. These one-dimensional flames offer a simple, fundamental configuration to improve the understanding of diffusion flame behavior and to explore such effects as

rical, burner-supported diffusion flames. These one-dimensional flames offer a simple, fundamental configuration to improve the understanding of diffusion flame behavior and to explore such effects as transport, kinetics, soot formation, and radiation, which can be more pronounced under microgravity conditions (Atreya et al. 1992; Law et al. 2001; Lecoustre et al. 2012). Spherically-symmetric flames are not generally practical in normal gravity. This can be explained by considering the Richardson number, which is the ratio of the buoyancy force to the inertial force, Ri = g (ΔT L) / (T u2) , (1) where g is the acceleration of gravity, T is temperature, L is the characteristic length scale, and u is the characteristic velocity. Taking as representative values L = 50 mm, u = 5 cm/s, ΔT = 2000 K, and T = 300 K, Ri = 1300 in normal gravity. Ri can be reduced with a judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity using low pressure hydrogen inverse flames. However for typical spherical diffusion flames the only way to obtain Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude. This requires a microgravity env

y using low pressure hydrogen inverse flames. However for typical spherical diffusion flames the only way to obtain Ri << 1 is to reduce g by four orders of magnitude. This requires a microgravity environment. Available microgravity drop tower facilities do not offer sufficient time to observe quasi-steady spherical diffusion flames, let alone their radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Experiments performed in the 5 s drop facility confirm that typical spherical diffusion flames continue growing during 5 s (see Fig. 2). Observations of cool flames in the FLEX, FLEX-2, and CFI droplet experiments involved or will involve burn times of up to 60 s. Analytical work supports these observations of slow flame development. Radial velocities in spherical diffusion flames scale with 1 / r2, where r is radius. Thus, at only a few burner diameters distance from the sphere, diffusion is the dominant transport mechanism. The characteristic diffusion time is r2/D, where D is mass diffusivity. For r = 25 mm and D = 20 mm2/s, this diffusion time is 30 s. Decreasing the flame size can reduce this time, but will not permit the observation of radiative extinction followed by cool di

Decreasing the flame size can reduce this time, but will not permit the observation of radiative extinction followed by cool diffusion flames. Our analytical and numerical calculations indicate that approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach quasi-steady state for these flames. The ISS is the only microgravity platform that can provide this environment.

ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter. As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm). Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers. The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface. The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for precise positioning.

The chamber insert includes three mass flow controllers (visible on the left of Fig. 2) for the delivery of fuel, oxidizer or inert (e.g., helium or carbon dioxide), and nitrogen to the burner. ACME’s primary flame diagnostics are a suite of imaging systems including five video cameras and two illumination systems, of which three cameras are part of the CIR facility and are already in use on orbit. All but one of the cameras is mounted outside of the chamber. Collectively, the imaging systems will enable color, CH*, and OH* imaging; pyrometry; measurement of the soot volume fraction; and operational support. Summary of Preliminary Results Abstract for Spherical Gas-Fueled Cool Diffusion Flames: An improved understanding of cool diffusion flames could lead to improved engines. CDFs are investigated here using a spherical porous burner with gaseous fuels in the microgravity environment of the International Space Station. Normal and inverse flames burning ethane, propane, and n-butane were explored with various fuel and oxygen concentrations, pressures, and flow rates. The diagnostics included an intensified video camera, radiometers, and thermocouples. Spherical CDFs burning gases were observed for the first time. However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39. The hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large. An analytical model is presented that combines previous models for steady droplet burning and the partial-burning regime for CDFs. The results identify the importance of burner temperature on the behavior of these CDFs. They also indicate that the observed CDFs reside in rich regions near a mixture fraction of 0.53.

Abstract for Cool Diffusion Flames in a Stably Stratified Stagnation Flow: Cool diffusion flames have been a growing research topic since their discovery in 2012. Until now their study has been hindered by the high cost of the experimental systems used to observe them. A method is presented here for observing CDFs inexpensively using a pool of liquid n-heptane and parallel plates heated so as to produce a stably stratified stagnation flow. The flames were imaged with a color camera and measurements included gas phase temperatures, fuel evaporation rates, and formaldehyde emissions. These are the first observations of CDFs burning near the surface of fuel pools. The measured peak temperatures were between 705 – 760 K, which corresponds to an increase in gas temperature of 70 K. Autoignition first occurred at 550 K. Cantera autoignition simulations for homogeneous mixtures with the CRECK mechanism predicted a cool flame temperature of 885 K, which is significantly higher than observed.

Impacts, Benefits, and Products Combustion provides 86% of the world’s energy and an even higher fraction of the energy used for transportation. The internal combustion engines used for transportation generally have thermal efficiencies of 38% or lower because of thermal losses. These efficiencies may increase to 60% if future engines can take advantage of ultra-lean combustion. Introduction Tests for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment are conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical

eady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of combustion and thermal transport processes.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 29 Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. In this regard, the CFI camera was developed for the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) which preceded ACME and studied non-premixed cool flames in the combustion of liquid droplets. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy- driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames ar

stics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol The CFI-G investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded

r each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. Introduction Tests for the Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) experiment are conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. As explained in the research proposal: Cool diffusion flames were discovered during droplet experiments aboard the International Space Station (ISS) in 2012, and this initiated a rapidly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progre

dly growing field of combustion research. Droplet experiments necessarily involve unsteady burning rates, so cool diffusion flames have never been observed as steady spherical flames. A natural progression toward understanding cool diffusion flames is to observe quasi-steady spherical flames on porous burners, and this is the topic of this proposal. The flames to be studied are rich in the physics and chemistry of combustion and thermal transport processes.

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 36 Most internal combustion engines are designed using computer models that neglect cool flame chemistry, but ignition and flame propagation in engines depend on cool flame chemistry. Cool flame chemistry also has a significant impact on fuel octane and cetane numbers, whose understanding has large economic consequences. The flame system to be studied will allow steady spherical cool diffusion flames to be observed for the first time. The tests, performed with gaseous fuel and a porous spherical burner, cannot be performed in normal gravity or in ground-based microgravity facilities. CFI-G had the following experimental hypotheses and experimental objective when it was proposed in 2017: Hypotheses The hypotheses of this research are that testing aboard the ISS can demonstrate the following for the first time, contributing to an improved understanding of cool flame kinetics. 1. Steady-state cool diffusion flames on spherical porous burners. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames fo

. 2. Cool diffusion flames burning propane, n-butane, and n-pentane. 3. Cool diffusion flames for a wide range of Zst, Tad, and pressures. 4. Inverse cool diffusion flames. 5. Cool diffusion flames for which a decrease in fluent flow rate will cause extinction, whereas an increase will cause a transition to a hot diffusion flame, with oscillation possible between hot and cool flames. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. where Zst and Tad are respectively the stochiometric mixture fraction and adiabatic flame temperature. However, it was later determined that the CIR facility could not support testing with pentane because of the fuel’s low vapor pressure so the test matrix was revised to instead include testing with ethane in addition to the propane and n-butane. The additional research objectives are as follows, where CFD stands for Computational Fluid Dynamics. B. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. C. The experiment is carried out using the same spherical burner configuration as ACME’s Flame Design and s-Flame (Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames) experiments. The instrumentation is the same as that used for Flame Design except that an alternate radiometer array was developed for CFI-G. Furthermore, the CFI-G tests were conducted using the

ACME/CFI-G Final Report (2022) 21 November 2022 37 formaldehyde filter on the CFI intensified camera rather than the typically used CH* filter. In this regard, the CFI camera was developed for the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) which preceded ACME and studied non-premixed cool flames in the combustion of liquid droplets. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy- driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames ar

stics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. VI. Summary of the ISS data collection The CFI-G data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other ACME experiments. To be clear, there was no collection of soot or other physical samples that were subsequently transported to the ground. The CFI-G image data includes images from the following cameras: 1. ACME DataCam, used with a clear fused-silica ‘filter’ and various zoom and focus settings (but those settings were consistent within each individual test) 2. CFI intensified camera, used always (or at least nearly so) with a formaldehyde filter for CFI-G 3. High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera, equipped with a red filter corresponding to the opposing CIR illumination package, which was sometimes left off The raw DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI, and HiBMs cameras are provided in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software Interfac

rast, the analog video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. Derek Dunn-Rankin of the University of California, Irvine (UC Irvine). Dr. Yu-Chien (Alice) Chien, also of UC Irvine, served as the Project Scientist at the university. Meanwhile, Dennis P. Stocker of the NASA Glenn Research Center is NASA’s Project Scientist (PS) for ACME including E-FIELD Flames and the rest of the ACME investigations. In preparatory drop testing, etc., Dr. Fumiaki Takahashi of the Case Western Reserve University (CWRU) served as the Deputy Project Scientist. For ACME’s spaceflight operations, the NASA science team includes Drs. Uday G. Hegde and Vedha Nayagam who are also with CWRU. Science Overview A. Background With minor editing, this background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document (SRD) of March 2010. This project utilizes electric fields in microgravity combustion science to establish a fundamental understanding of chemi-ionization and ion-driven convection in flames. It also uses this understanding to demonstrate electrical manipulation of sooting behavior and stability limits in the absence of buoyancy. This work is based on prior foundation studies that included simulating zero-g combustion of small gas jet diffusion flames in an earth-gravity laboratory, and the electric field control of flame electrodynamics. The current SRD proposes to use the extended-duration microgravity environment to further

jet diffusion flames in an earth-gravity laboratory, and the electric field control of flame electrodynamics. The current SRD proposes to use the extended-duration microgravity environment to further develop an understanding of electric fields in combustion processes and their potential applications.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 4 The research centers on the fact that electrical forces, acting on charge carriers created through chemi-ionization, can provide for measurement and manipulation of flames in microgravity environments. For example, using the drag exercised on flame ions, electric fields have demonstrated observable influences on flame shape, sooting behavior, burning velocity, extinction, and stability. The source of these influences almost certainly resides in ion wind effects. In microgravity, where there are no density-driven buoyant effects to contend with, ion winds represent an important (and perhaps the only) body force that can be applied to manipulate combustion systems. This project includes both academic study of electric field effects and aspects for practical utilization of electrical control of combustion processes. The prior laboratory experiments have shown that electrical properties of flames can be used to produce enhanced combustion performance by: (a) manipulating flame ions in order to change flame chemistry – this is generally considered a minor influence because flame ion concentration is typically small, but it may be c

tion performance by: (a) manipulating flame ions in order to change flame chemistry – this is generally considered a minor influence because flame ion concentration is typically small, but it may be critical at near-limit conditions; (b) creating a neutral wind (ion driven convection) locally at the flame front – this process can provide a local actuator for flame convection control; (c) using electric fields to affect soot formation and transport – ions and soot are closely linked because there are shared chemical pathways and because soot particles are charged by the flame ions; and (d) using electrical properties to characterize flames – e.g., there is a relationship between flame temperature, the carbon content of a fuel, and the ion current it can produce at saturation. In 1-g, the above-mentioned processes are confounded by complex buoyancy interactions that cannot be unraveled. Hence, to evaluate them in detail, we propose the following experimental objectives for an extended microgravity environment: (A) determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel; (B) com

crogravity environment: (A) determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel; (B) compare the time response of the flame’s chemiluminescence and ion current to rapid changes in electric fields; (C) determine sooting behavior in relation to the electric field influences; and (D) manipulate the limit behavior of lifted flames using electric fields. The experimental approach includes a simple gas jet diffusion flame and a co-flow burner. The basic variations in the tests are in the burner type, the fuel type (nominally nonsooting and sooting), and in the level of inert dilution of the fuel to vary the flame strength. The co-flow or environment gas will have a nominal molar composition of 21% O2 and 79% N2. The experimental concept is to ground the burner to the test chamber and to install an electrically active planar mesh electrode downstream of the burner mouth. The potential of the mesh electrode can be either positive or negative, with a steady voltage or with a time varying potential (including a rapid step change) to examine the flame’s steady state response and tim

al of the mesh electrode can be either positive or negative, with a steady voltage or with a time varying potential (including a rapid step change) to examine the flame’s steady state response and time response. The data to be recorded include the applied voltage, the ion current, the flame broadband luminosity, the CH* luminosity, flame images of OH* and visible light showing the flame shape as a function of electric potential and flame shape changes during transients in the electric field. In addition, a desired measurement of temperature in and near the flame will monitor the thermal field as a function of the electric field conditions. The data from these measurements will allow a chemical and physical understanding of flame ion production and information showing the potential to use these ions to electrically control the flame both via modification of the local chemistry near extinction limits and through changes in the local convection using the ion driven wind. For example, a lifted diffusion flame near its blowoff condition is sensitive to mixing at the flame anchor point. Therefore, electric fields acting

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 5 on near-limit flames can exert a large influence because they can affect the local mixing behavior. The role of electric fields on soot formation will be dramatic under conditions where the ion driven wind has a large influence on flow residence time (or on ion residence time, if chemical effects are found important) in sooting flames. Generally, the convective flows driven by electric fields acting on flame ions and those driven by buoyancy have been found to be of the same order of magnitude in earth gravity. In addition, raising the temperature often increases the ion production rate and the response to an electric field, but increasing temperature also increases the buoyancy effect, making it difficult, on earth, to separate ion wind effects from those due to buoyancy. In the zero-g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and develop sufficient understanding to predict the response of flames to electric fields under all conditions. In addition, exploring instabilities and extinction behavior in near-limit flames requires experiments lasting tens of seconds. Overall, the goal of this zero-gravity study is to understand chemi-ionization behavior and the resulting ion driven winds sufficiently well so that electrical properties of flames can be used to characterize (by monitoring ion current) and control them (via direct chemical or local convective influences). Electric field effects on flames have been documented for decades (even centuries), but flames in 1-g all include buoyancy influences that affect ion generation behavior. As described in the Background and Overview (Section 1.1), electric field effects and buoyancy effects have been found to be of the same order of magnitude. In addition, in some cases, raising the flame temperature will increase the O atom concentration, thereby increasing the ion production rate and increasing the response to an electric field. to separate ion wind effects from buoyancy. In the zero-g environment, it will be possible to eliminate the buoyancy confusion and develop sufficient understanding to predict the response of flames to electric fields under all conditions. For electrically driven flames, microgravity is also necessary to create conditions that produce symmetric flames suitable for Abel inversion and steady-state analysis. While in general natural convection can enhance symmetry relative to non-buoyant flames, a flame at 1-g in an electric wind experiences buoyancy as a disruptive influence on symmetry. Even when buoyancy effects can be minimized, we have found that there are periodic disturbances that disrupt the ideal symmetry. Highly symmetric conditions of extended microgravity are also useful for numerically simulating these various effects by our electrokinetic model or more comprehensively by others.

The ultimate objective of this experiment is to develop an understanding of the mechanisms of chemi-ionization in flames and to describe the interplay between convective flows driven by those flame ions and their generation rate. With this information it will then be possible to detect and control flame behavior electrically. In 1-g, laminar diffusion flames are often controlled to a large extent by natural convection, and particularly by the rate at which natural convection brings fresh oxidizer to the reactio

ectrically. In 1-g, laminar diffusion flames are often controlled to a large extent by natural convection, and particularly by the rate at which natural convection brings fresh oxidizer to the reaction zone. Hence, the vigor with which combustion proceeds depends on local convection. As described in Section 1, an electric field acting on flame ions produces a body force and convection (analogous to buoyancy) which affects the combustion process. The change in the combustion process can in turn affect the ion production rate, which is responsible for the body force. This coupled interaction is very difficult to measure, study, and understand in 1-g because buoyant forces (of approximately equal magnitude) interfere. In microgravity, there is no such complication and the body force in the flame is associated entirely with the ion-driven wind. 1-g experiments have demonstrated clearly that electrically driven convection can be used to modify the local flow field in a manner that changes combustion behavior. For example, it can stabilize lifted flames or force them to reattach. Electric fields have been seen to change soot formation,

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 8 though whether solely by residence time effects or their combination with chemical alterations has not been confirmed. In addition, ions can attach to soot particles providing them with enhanced mobility that can be manipulated. Furthermore, the electrical properties of flames provide a measure of their character. For example, non-premixed flames exhibit different relationships between ion production and ion wind forces than do premixed flames. The hydrocarbon fuel, and in particular, the carbon/hydrogen ratio, also affects these interactions. The goal of this project is to clarify and quantify this range of electrical effects and to then demonstrate the electrical manipulation of flame stability and soot in flames using the information obtained. To accomplish this scientific goal, there are four fundamental experimental objectives, in priority order, using a jet diffusion flame burner and a co-flow diffusion flame burner. The jet flame is the more critical configuration because it has a large 1-g data foundation and it can be more easily modeled as an ion and thermal source. These data provide the dynamic system behavior of the flame. This information comprises the time response of the flame (i.e., its surface area and luminosity) as compared to the time response of the ion current. These timescales can temporally separate the direct chemical effects of electric fields from ion diffusion and ion wind convective forcing. ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 9 The interaction between soot and electric fields is very complex because it combines the direct influence of electric fields on the chemistry, the ion wind effects on residence time and mixing, and the electric forces on the charged soot particles themselves. The zero-gravity environment, using the combination of the jet diffusion flame and the co-flow flame provides a wide range of conditions where these different influences can be allowed to dominate individually. For example, the forced convection environment of the co-flow burner will minimize the influence of the axial ion-driven wind, which helps to distinguish the direct electrical effects on ion chemistry in soot formation. In addition to demonstrating the direct control of soot behavior by electric fields, separating the influences can help distinguish between neutral molecule addition mechanisms of soot formation and those that presume the importance of ionic species. For example, changing the strength and polarity of the electric field can change the availability of ion precursors, and electric convection can manipulate reactants’ time/temperature history. In additi

r example, changing the strength and polarity of the electric field can change the availability of ion precursors, and electric convection can manipulate reactants’ time/temperature history. In addition, charges will accumulate onto soot, and the electric field can then act directly on the soot particles to change their residence time and path through the flame. D) Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. Because the chemi-ion current per unit flame area can be used as an indicator of flame strength, its measure (both average and fluctuating properties) with low electric field voltage can be used to detect flames approaching their limit condition. By adjusting the electric field, 1-g studies indicate that an ion driven wind can be used to reduce the liftoff height and stabilize the flame. This is an example of open loop electrical flame sensing, analysis, and control.

The E-FIELD Flames experiment is being conducted in 2018 within the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) [15], which was launched in 2008 and used from 2009 to 2017 for a series of droplet combustion experiments [16]. The CIR facility is similar in size to a vending machine as can be seen in Figure 1. It includes a 100-liter combustion chamber capable of operation at pressures of up to 300 kPa. The chamber features a ring of 8 sapphire windows and is equipped with a set of reconfigurable imaging systems. The CIR was designed with gas delivery, venting, thermal control, electrical power, data handling, image processing and storage, and vibration isolation to enable combustion research with gaseous, liquid, and solid fuels.

Hardware Shortcomings As previously discussed, the slow response time of the high-voltage power supplies (recommended in the ISRD) did not meet the requirements necessary to achieve the requested time response performance, and as such inhibited determination of the flame’s response time to rapid changes in the electric field strength. The negative and positive high-voltage power supplies were to have been coupled, as described for example in Appendix C of the ISRD. However, switching between the two high-voltage power supplies led to excessive Electromagnetic Interference (EMI) so the power supplies were completely decoupled, where only one was installed at a time. For most ACME experiments, the limiting gas constraint is the oxygen/nitrogen bottles used to fill the chamber. This resource constraint is exacerbated by the CIR because it is equipped with a pair of redundant safety timers to limit the fuel that can flow into the combustion chamber (where the timers can be set for the oxidizer flow in the case of inverse flame testing). surrounded by a weak coflow of ‘air’ which also fills the chamber, but where tests are also conducted with no coflow. A test includes starting the gas flows to prime the system, energizing the igniter to initiate a flame, retracting the igniter, and allowing the flame to steady slightly before energizing the electric field to its initial value. The flame is again allowed to steady before beginning a voltage sweep over a specified range with steps or smooth ramps of specified voltage changes and durations. Hegde, U. and D. Dunn-Rankin, “Ion Current and Flame Changes with Electric Fields in Microgravity,” 11th U.S. National Combustion Meeting 2019, Pasadena, CA, 24-27 March 2019. This work presents changes in reaction zone shape and location, as well as ion currents obtained after applying an electric field onto a diffusion flame with fuel dilution in the International Space Station (ISS). As one of the projects of Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME), the E-FIELD Flames experiments were initiated in March and completed in November of 2018 with a series of flame studies on the coflow burner and the jet burner within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR). The coflow burner, presented in this paper, consists of a small central fuel jet and a concentric outer ring flowing with synthetic air. The research examines fundamental hydrocarbon flame behaviors driven by the chemi-ion response during the combustion process. The expe

fuel jet and a concentric outer ring flowing with synthetic air. The research examines fundamental hydrocarbon flame behaviors driven by the chemi-ion response during the combustion process. The experiment is conducted by applying high voltage onto a copper mesh situated 37 mm above the burner tip, where measurements include images and ion currents over a range of electric field strengths and time histories depending on the region of interest (e.g., near the saturation transition). This paper specially investigates the flame behavior while flowing different methane/nitrogen mixture compositions. Among other effects, the results show that the electric field can stabilize the microgravity diffusion flame at very high dilution conditions, especially when there is no coflowing air. The preliminary results are discussed in greater detail in sections based on the burner configuration (coflow burner and jet burner), fuel (methane and ethylene), and dilution levels tested. Field direction and polarities The electric field is established between the two electrodes, burner and mesh, which are connected separately with positive and negative polarity, as the test requires. Because this research has no gravitationally relevant direction, any orientation can serve as the spatial reference coordinate. The vast majority of research in electric field related combustion study is conducted at earth gravity, where the buoyancy is one of the key properties considered and repeatedly discussed. In microgravity, a facing upright burner is equivalent to one facing upside down (or even sideways) scientifically because the buoyancy/gravitation force is zero. Surprises and New Discoveries We expect many more discoveries to arise as we sort through the detailed data sets, but the initial surprises and discoveries include: (1) The behavior of the V-I curve is distinctly different in microgravity as compared to 1-g flames, where in microgravity there is not a distinctive saturation ion current plateau but rather the flames exhibit a distinct peak ion current that corresponds to the most compact flame. These results show that buoyancy driven flows are an important influence on 1-g flames even when an electric field is applied. (2) When soot is present in a flame, electric fields create a wide range of unpredictable behaviors that include elimination of the soot through what appears to be enhanced mixing for combustion, showers of luminous particles that are likely to be incandescent soot agglomerates, and unstable dancing flames. Sooting is far more significant in flames in microgravity than is seen in simi

bustion, showers of luminous particles that are likely to be incandescent soot agglomerates, and unstable dancing flames. Sooting is far more significant in flames in microgravity than is seen in similar conditions with 1-g flames. (3) There are clear correlations between flame luminosity, combustion intensity, and ion current. The results suggest that the most robust burning also produces the highest ion current, even though the flame is most compact. (4) The very weak low fuel concentration flames were stabilized at ignition with very small electric fields, where without the fields the flames would quickly quench. This stabilizing feature of electric fields for weak zero gravity flames was a surprise, and it suggests that electric fields may be a good tool for approximating buoyancy body forces at partial gravity. (5) Jet flames under the influence of the electric field were unstable at high field strengths, and these flames experienced corona and then arc discharges due to the large field concentration near the jet burner tip. The flame behavior was dramatic but difficult to characterize, suggesting a spatially- and time-varying field/flame interaction.

Introduction The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. In this experiment, an electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts is established between the burner and a flat, circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. The motion of the charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong electric field. The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting behavior of the flame. Measurements are made of electric-field strength, the ion current passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis of ion-d

rough the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity allows for great simplifications in the analysis of ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 44 An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer. The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical benefit. For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel-lean conditions with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the electric field. As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic. It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame. The experiment contributes to our critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: A. Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e.,

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 45 gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Microgravity flame flicker is then the result of electric body forces alone. Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum- dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be

a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or soot limit. This was not done during Increments 55-56, where the console commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

Preliminary Research Findings Results from the early E-FIELD Flame experiments have demonstrated clear differences between normal-gravity and microgravity flame behaviors. A few examples include the distinct maximum of ion current for co-flow burner flames in microgravity, where the 1-g flames more smoothly reach a saturation condition. This curve provides information on the flames ability to produce chemi-ions based on its saturation ion current, and it provides a measure of combustion performance in that ion production is a function of carbon influx into the flame and the vigorousness of the combustion process. Introduction The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment was conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project. In this experiment, an electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts was established between the burner and a flat, circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner. The motion of the charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong electric field. The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting behavior of the flam

which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong electric field. The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting behavior of the flame. Measurements were made of electric-field strength, the ion current passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability. Conducting the tests in microgravity allowed for great simplifications in the

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 59 analysis of ion-driven convection and flame interaction, enabling new understanding and the development of less polluting and more efficient combustion technology for use on Earth. An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer. The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical benefit. For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel-lean conditions with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the electric field. As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic. It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame. The experiment contributes to our critical understand

pears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame. The experiment contributes to our critical understanding of combustion processes in the presence of electric fields. More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives: A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel. B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted f

e and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream. D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven wind to stabilize or reattach these flames. The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of flame and electric field conditions. The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric-field voltage and polarity were the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment. Tests were conducted with methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of soot-producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting. They were carried out with both a simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment. Tests with the coflow burner were conducted with and without a coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame. The coflow burner also provided a different electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-

e latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame. The coflow burner also provided a different electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane). In a typical test, the mesh electrode was energized at increasing potentials (relative to the burner), where the flame’s response (e.g., ion current, luminosity, shape) to the resulting field strength was measured. The field strength was changed in repeated steps or was instead smoothly ramped.

ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 60 Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies. For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy- driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Therefore, the flicker in the E-FIELD Flames was a result of electric body forces alone. Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis. Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal- gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electroni

e soot free. The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application. II. Methods/Research Operations A. Discussion of Method/Protocol E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However

ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts. However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream. For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or soot limit. This was not done during Increments 55-56 or 57-58, where the console commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished. Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment. Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

infrequent, but there are some days when tests aborted repeatedly. Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite. The first test of the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been sufficiently primed. Ignition was sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of the igniter glow rather than a flame. As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite. This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module. The OH* chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum. However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to false ignition detection. E. Preliminary Research Findings Distinctly different results were seen in E-FIELD Flames’ second round tests with the gas- jet burner when compared with the first round tests with the coflow burner. For example, the ion current response to the electric field strength with an upward ion driven wind in microgravity is a clear parabolic trend (which is similar to the trend observed in 1-g flames with the coflow burner as presented in the prior report). The parabolic behavior is evident even with the strong oscillati

a clear parabolic trend (which is similar to the trend observed in 1-g flames with the coflow burner as presented in the prior report). The parabolic behavior is evident even with the strong oscillations observed during the rise. This rising trend is not observed with the coflow burner. The behavior of the soot and its charge state are complicated since in the regions of high field strength, particularly near the fuel tube where the field lines converge, soot can emit or collect free charges. Hence, the soot transport is driven directly by the field and by the ion-driven wind (and thermophoresis) which means it can travel differentially to the bulk flow. These various transport elements can push the soot through the flame to burnout, hold it in stasis in the flame for additional growth, or drive it to the burner where it accumulates. More work is needed to sort through these elements. This report shows the initial results of the E-FIELD Flames experiment using the gas-jet burner in the International Space Station (ISS). The positive field allows the soot to concentrate and compresses the flame into a high current density thermal source. The flames demonstrate an unpredicted oscillation before extinguishing with increasing field strength. This oscillating phenomenon was not observed during the tests with the coflow burner from the first round, with the exception of a case that introduced the airflow at 30 cm/s which increased the surface reaction while the flame tended to balance between electric field effects, io

rner from the first round, with the exception of a case that introduced the airflow at 30 cm/s which increased the surface reaction while the flame tended to balance between electric field effects, ions, and charged soot. The negative field allows the flame to maintain its spherical characteristic in microgravity. The yellow soot appears for both of the electric field directions within the flame around the tip and disappears with increasing field strength after reaching the current peak. The role of soot in the i-v behavior of these flames requires further investigation. Early E-FIELD Flame results from the ISS testing were presented in following oral and poster presentations: 1. E-FIELD Flames studies how electric fields at different voltages influence flames. An electric field can strongly influence the motion of the ions produced by a combustion reaction. This first day was very successful with ten flames ignited for studying the effects of an electric field on laminar diffusion flames. Preliminary results show that the high-voltage electric field created forces similar to buoyancy, which dramatically affected the flame’s shape, intensity, and soot production. e high-voltage electric field created forces similar to buoyancy, which dramatically affected the flame’s shape, intensity, and soot production. g ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting behavior of the flame. ACME/E-FIELD Flames Final Report (2019) 10 April 2021 97 Appendix J. Summary of the ISS data collection The E-FIELD Flames data is all digital and includes both image and non-image data, where this is true for the other current ACME experiments. To be clear, there is no collection of soot or other physical samples that are subsequently transported to the ground. The E-FIELD Flames image data includes images from the ACME DataCam, the CFI intensified camera (used with the CH* filter), and the High-Bitdepth Multispectral (HiBMs) camera (equipped with a red filter corresponding to the opposing CIR illumination package). The DataCam images are in a Halcon Iconic Object (hobj) format, while the images from the CFI and HiBMs cameras are in a Tagged Image File (tif) format. In contrast, the analog video was recorded on the ground in a Transport Stream (ts) format. The key non-imaging data from a test is a comma-delimited file that is described in detail in the Software Interface Design Description (ACME-DOC-010 Rev. D). The data is currently archived at NASA and work is underway to make it available publicly through NASA’s Physical Science Informatics System (PSI).

Background This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document (SRD) of April 2010. The majority of practical combustion processes involve nonpremixed combustion of hydrocarbons. These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these tech

t be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing pressures, but these techniques generally weaken flames, leading to performance penalties and possible extinction. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address

ACME/Flame Design Final Report (2023) 6 April 2023 4 these concerns. The approach is termed flame design, as it takes a fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent constraints imposed, designs flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. Flame design involves affecting the basic structure of the flame in that the relationship between the temperature and concentration fields is varied to accomplish a stated objective. The method involves exchanging nitrogen (or any inert, including carbon dioxide) from the oxidizer stream to the fuel stream such that the stoichiometric mixture fraction, Zst, can be varied with or without affecting adiabatic flame temperature, Tad. The structure of a high Zst flame is substantially different from that of the standard hydrocarbon/air flame, where Zst is relatively low. By varying Zst at constant Tad, flames have been produced that are soot-free at any strain rate (permanently blue) and have extinction scalar dissipation rates up to 40 times those of their fuel-air counterparts. The nitrogen exchange approach (or some variant of it) has been the subject of many studies by the PI and Co-Is (Du and Axelbaum, 19

sipation rates up to 40 times those of their fuel-air counterparts. The nitrogen exchange approach (or some variant of it) has been the subject of many studies by the PI and Co-Is (Du and Axelbaum, 1995, 1996, Chao et al., 1998, Sunderland et al., 2003, 2004, Liu et al., 2005, Chen and Axelbaum, 2005, Kumfer et al., 2006, 2008, Santa et al., 2007a, 2007b, Skeen et al., 2009) and other investigators (Sung et al., 1995; Lin and Faeth, 1996; Kang et al., 1997; Hwang and Chung, 2001). Although these studies have been informative, they typically involved normal-gravity flames, where buoyancy and inherent strain complicated the interpretation of results. For example, these ambiguities have led to different theories to explain the phenomenon of permanently-blue diffusion flames. It is not known whether this phenomenon is due more to a change in the direction of convection across the flame or to a change in the detailed structure of the flame. This issue can be addressed by performing microgravity experiments because the unique character of nonbuoyant microgravity flames allows the effects of convection direction and flame structure to be independently varied. By ejecting fuel into an oxid

By ejecting fuel into an oxidizer in a buoyancy free system, the convective flow across the flame is unambiguously from fuel to oxidizer. Alternatively, by ejecting oxidizer into fuel, the flow is from oxidizer to fuel. Furthermore, the long residence times that can be obtained in the spherical flame geometry will allow for validation of a theory that predicts the sooting limits at the limit of infinite Damköhler number, Da. Studies of the effect of Zst on scalar dissipation rate at extinction have indicated that there is a unique Zst where the flame is most resistant to extinction. These findings also suggest that by employing inert exchange to vary Zst, the peak temperature can be shifted to coincide with the location of radical production, thus allowing the flame to burn at much lower temperatures. The optimum minimum temperature at extinction has led us to propose the concept of a pseudo- flammability limit for nonpremixed flames. Again, this fundamental information is most unambiguously demonstrated in quasi-steady, microgravity flames wherein the effects of flame structure can be systematically studied. The proposed work will also allow, for the first time, a strain-free experimental study of the effects of Zst on soot inception and flame extinction processes. Microgravity experiments will involve gaseous hydrocarbon diffusion flames supported on porous spherical burners and coflow burners.1 Soot inception limits and flame extinction limits will be obtained as functions of Zst, amount of inert, flow direction, and pressure. The effect of flow direction across the flame will be studied by performing coflow experiments (desired) where the fuel issues into the oxidizer and oxidizer issues into fuel. Gas temperatures will be measured by thin film pyrometry and thermocouples to identify the soot- inception temperature. Previous ground-based microgravity experiments have demonstrated the value of the spherical, burner-supported nonpremixed flames for flame studies. The one-dimensional flame offers a simple, fundamental configuration to improve our understanding of nonpremixed flame behavior and to explore such effects as radiation and thermophoresis, which are more pronounced under microgravity conditions (Atreya et al., 1992, Law et al., 2001). The burner-supported spherical flame is in some respects similar to droplet burning but it holds the advantages that larger flames are possible and, with sufficiently long time, can approach quasi-steady state. Furthermore, the proposed microgravity coflow flames allow the direction of convection across the flame to be varied. Although the spherically-symmetric flame geometry has many advantages, it is not practical to produce such a flame at normal gravity. Although the spherically-symmetric flame geometry has many advantages, it is not practical to produce such a flame at normal gravity. The reason for this can be understood by considering the Richardson number, Ri, which is the ratio of the buoyancy force to the inertial force and is given by

In fact, it is much higher than this because the more appropriate length and velocity scales are the flame diameter and the velocity at the flame, respectively. The value of Ri can be reduced by judicious choice of fuels and inert; Law et al. (2001) have shown that nearly spherical flames can be created in normal gravity. However, Ri for these flames is still on the order of unity, implying that while the flames appear spherical, natural convection is still present. Furthermore, hydrogen must be used as a fuel and be supplied in the ambient so such flames are not relevant to this study. This can be accomplished in a number of microgravity environments, including ground-based facilities, e.g., drop towers for short times, as well as flight experiments, e.g., the International Space Station for longer times.
