Sample heating temperature derivation Sample heating temperature is one of the key parameters that dictate the properties of generated smoke particles. When studying effects of gravity on the smoke properties, we want to compare smokes generated at the same temperature. For SAME and SAMER, during a test, the software controls the temperature via the resistance of heating wire. It is true that for the same wire coil, constant wire resistance means constant wire temperature. Traditionally, test c

test, the software controls the temperature via the resistance of heating wire. It is true that for the same wire coil, constant wire resistance means constant wire temperature. Traditionally, test conditions are specified by Rt/R0, the ratio between the resistance of heated wire over the resistance of the wire at room temperature. Thus, before each run, the sample wire resistance is measured, then multiplied by this parameter to get the target resistance for the control circuitry. Although, Rt/R0 can uniquely define the temperature, it is not clear what actual sample temperature is. Since the wire resistance is one of the parameters that are logged in the engineering data sheet which makes it possible to derive actual temperature from the logged resistances. However, when deriving wire temperatures, one has to take the fact into account that the wire length varies from sample to sample and so called room temperature varies too. After the heating temperatures were obtained, it is surprising that for the same Rt/R0, the actual heating temperature difference can be as large as 30 degrees Celsius. The following is how this is carried out. SAME heater temperature modeling.

Objective: It was identified that each sample has a significant length of leading section of the resistive wire. This section does not touch the sample material and is exposed in air flow. Thus the temperature of this leading section is different from the portion of the wire that contacts the sample material. The control circuitry only controls the total resistance of the heating wire, not individual portion of the wire. Our goal is to find the temperature of the wire that is in contact with the sample material. Formulation: Hypothesis: the temperature difference between the two portions of the wire is caused by different convection heat transfer from the two. The wire that is in contact with the sample has less heat loss from the convection heat transfer because about half of its surface area is covered by the sample material. Assumptions and simplifications: 1) Assume the entire wire consists of two distinct portions, one is in air (portion 1) and the other (portion 2) is in touch with the sample so that only half of the wire area is exposed to air. 2) Uniform cross section area of the wire, so the resistance is proportional to the length and the resistivity of the wire. 3) Resis

th the sample so that only half of the wire area is exposed to air. 2) Uniform cross section area of the wire, so the resistance is proportional to the length and the resistivity of the wire. 3) Resistivity is a known function of temperature. 4) Temperature distribution inside wire is uniform. 5) Newton convective heat transfer equation applies to both sections but with different coefficients. Although the port 2 is half exposed in air where convective equation works and half in contact with sample where transient conduction heat transfer should be used, for the sake of simplicity, we lump the two mechanisms together and use convection only with a modified heat transfer coefficient. Cumulative moments for limited particle size range Theoretically, a lognormal distribution is defined in the particle size from zero to infinity, whereas any instrument used to measure certain moment of an aerosol inevitably has a limited particle size range. In some cases, an

distribution is defined in the particle size from zero to infinity, whereas any instrument used to measure certain moment of an aerosol inevitably has a limited particle size range. In some cases, an impacter is inserted in the inlet of an instrument to eliminate particles larger than certain size. In these cases, the instrument cannot sense the entire range of the distribution as the theory describes. Thus, one would like to know how much signal is lost due to the limited effective particle size range, or what the percentage of the total signal the instrument receives. This piece of information is useful to assess errors induced by omitting particles in a certain size range. It was found this question can be answered conveniently using the error function calculations, which is available in the Excel spread sheet or some other computational software or even in the tables of most mathematical handbooks. The following is the detailed discussion of how to do this. The reflight experiment built upon the results of the original flight during Expedition 15 by adding diagnostic measurements and expanding the test matrix. Five different materials representative of those found in spacecraft (Teflon, Kapton, cotton, silicone rubber and Pyrell) were heated to temperatures below the ignition point with conditions controlled to provide repeatable sample surface temperatures and air flow. The smoke was initially collected in an aging chamber to simulate the transport time from the smoke source to the detector. This effective transport time was varied by holding the smoke in the aging chamber for times ranging from 11 to 1800 s. I. Introduction ppropriate design of fire detection systems requires knowledge of both the expected signature of the events to be detected and the background levels of the measured parameters. Terrestrial fire detection systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires.1, 2 Unfortunately there is no corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently the fire detectors in current spacecraft were developed based upon terrestrial designs. There are a number of factors that can be expected to affect the particle size distribution of the smoke from spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravity increases the residence time in microgravity fires and increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector.3 Microgravity fires have been found to have radically different structure from their normal-gravity (a.k.a. 1-g) counterparts. The limited options available to respond to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of early detection. Finally the materials used in spacecraft are different from typical terrestrial applications where smoke properties were previously evaluated. All of these effects can be expected to change the smoke

Finally the materials used in spacecraft are different from typical terrestrial applications where smoke properties were previously evaluated. All of these effects can be expected to change the smoke particle size distribution. The objective of this work was to make sufficient measurements of smoke from spacecraft fires to enable improved design of future detectors. Smoke Background Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes. In particular it can include unburned, recondensed, original polymer or pyrolysis products that can be either liquid or solid, hydrocarbon soot, condensed water vapor, and ash particles. Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate in established flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fire growth. Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot. Prior spacecraft systems are summarized in more detail in papers by Friedman and Urban.4, 5 In the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo missions, the crew quarters were limited and mission durations were short, consequently it was considered reasonable that the astronauts would rapidly detect any fire. The Skylab module, however, included approximately 30 UV-sensing fire detectors.4 These devices were limited to line-of-sight and were reported to have difficulties with false alarms. The Space Shuttle Detectors were based upon ionization fire detector technology, the most advanced technology available at the time and used an inertial separator designed to eliminate particles larger than 1-2 micrometers. The International Space Station (ISS) smoke detectors use near-IR forward scattering, rendering them most sensitive to particles larger than a micrometer, outside of the range of sensitivity of the shuttle detector. As described by Friedman4 there have been six overheat and failed component events in the NASA Orbiter fleet in addition to several similar incidents t

he range of sensitivity of the shuttle detector. As described by Friedman4 there have been six overheat and failed component events in the NASA Orbiter fleet in addition to several similar incidents that have occurred on the ISS. None of these events spread into a real fire but as mission durations increase, the likelihood of failures increases. The experience on Mir in 1997 has shown that failure of oxygen generation systems can have significant consequences. As a result, improved understanding of spacecraft fire detection is critically needed.6 Previous work on smoke particles from low-gravity sources by Urban et al.5 found that the particulate produced by low-gravity flames (soot or unburned fuel particles) tends to have larger size particles than in normal gravity. Results from the CSD (Comparative Soot Diagnostics) Experiment5 which studied smoke properties in low-gravity from several spacecraft materials suggested that liquid smoke particles could achieve sizes larger than 1 µm while solid particulate remained in the sub-micrometer range. However, the CSD experiment did not produce sufficient data concerning the size of the liquid smoke particles to guide detector design. The

hile solid particulate remained in the sub-micrometer range. However, the CSD experiment did not produce sufficient data concerning the size of the liquid smoke particles to guide detector design. The combined impact of these limited results and theoretical predictions is that, as opposed to extrapolation from 1-g data, direct knowledge of low-g combustion particulate is needed for more confident design of smoke detectors for spacecraft. II. SAME Experiment To address the limited data from the CSD experiment concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke particulate, another experiment was developed: the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). The SAME experiment sought to avoid the problems experienced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. This is a challenging endeavor because existing aerosol instrumentation is typically large, incompatible with spacecraft experiment constraints, and some systems require substantial sample return to Earth. As will be described below, an alternative approach was employed that used three discrete instruments to measure separate moments of the size distribution. When combined, these moments provide useful aggregate statistics of the size distribution. The measurements were made using smoke generated by overheated spacecraft materials in much the same manner as the CSD experiment however the sample temperature, flow field, and particle aging time were more rigorously controlled in the SAME experiment. These were comprised of samples of 6 materials: Teflon™, Kapton™, Pyrell™, silicone rubber, cellulose (lamp wick), and dibutyl-phthalate deposited on a porous wick. The test conditions included multiple sample temperatures and air flow rates. The baseline air flow rate was 8 cm/s with runs conducted at rates down to 2 cm/s with a limited set conducted with no airflow while the sample was heated. The sample temperatures were based on the pyrolysis properties of the material and were thus material specific. The baseline temperature was selected to produce 1 to 2 mg of weight loss in 60 seconds and have reasonable signal on each of the moment instruments. 2. MPASS Results The MPASS was included in SAME-2 to demonstrate the effectiveness of a two-moment smoke detector. Because of how they are used, a smoke detector is not calibrated for specific materials and instead has a single calibration for all conditions. The objective is to maintain a flat sensor response, regardless of the type of smoke or the particle size so the signal is proportional only to a selected moment (e.g. mass or number concentration). The approach used was to derive correlations to predict the smoke number concentration and mass concentration from the MPASS output. This correlation was made using the other SAME measurements (number and mass concentration) as a reference. A least-squares, third-order, correlation was computed on all test points with a signal to noise ratio greater than 2 independent of all other parameters (e.g. material, heating rate, and aging time). The results are shown in figures 9 and 10, for prediction of the mass concentration and the number concentration, respectively. Ideally these response graphs should be horizontal lines. 4. Impact of flow on particle morphology As the samples are heated by the wire, chemical bonds are broken and gaseous products are released via pyrolysis. These products may include partially oxidized species resulting from the reaction with oxygen. As the gases move from the wire, the temperature and species concentration will decrease as a result of conduction/diffusion and convection. With the decrease in temperature, the super saturation ratio of the pyrolysis gas will pass a critical stage and nucleation of smoke particles will occur. These smoke nuclei grow rapidly from the condensation of the pyrolysis gases. The time scale for the nucleation and condensation is on the order of ms or less. Over a longer time scale, the growing smoke particles undergoing Brownian motion collide and stick together in a process known as coagulation. This process may continue for time scales of up to 103 s. If the particles are liquid, the colliding particles will coalesce and form larger droplets. This is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig. 11). If the particles are solid, they will retain their structure as they stick resulting in an agglomerate structure compos

This is the case for the lampwick, silicone rubber, and Kapton smokes (Fig. 11). If the particles are solid, they will retain their structure as they stick resulting in an agglomerate structure composed of many primary particles connected in a low density fractal- like structure. This is the case for the Teflon and Pyrell smokes (Fig. 11). Key parameters affecting the smoke properties of the smoke produced here are the low-gravity condition, the convective flow past the heated wire, the wire temperature, and the aging time. As the wire temperature increases, more of the sample will be pyrolyzed and these gases will subsequently condense on the nuclei leading to a larger mass concentration of the aerosol and a larger diameter of average mass. An increase in the convective flow for a fixed wire temperature is expected to result in an increase in the pyrolysis rate and thus an increase in the mass concentration of the aerosol. Some results follow this trend with silicone rubber, lampwick, and Pyrell increasing slightly with flow while Teflon and Kapton decrease. Although these are expected to be small variations, given the exponential dependence of the pyrolysis kinetics on temperature, changes in the heat transport environment could change the sample surface temperature between the wire coils. A case of special interest is the case of zero-flow. The transport for the zero-flow case in μ-g is controlled by molecular diffusion and thermal expansion. Over a period of 60 seconds, the gases would diffuse a distance on the order of 4 cm. Assuming a cubical geometry this would correspond to the smoke being confined to a volume of about 64 cm3 rather than being diluted in the 6000 cm3 piston. If the same number of particles is generated as for the flow case, the initial concentration will be on the order of 50 times higher for the zero-flow case. This is expected to lead to more coagulation and a larger particle size. It is found for all of the materials the diameter of average mass is 30 % to 40 % larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests. The zero flow condition was not in the original design of the SAME hardware but was examined for 11 tests by modifying the valve operation in the SAME hardware. This resulted in a very high concentration of particulate where the aging process was accelerated compared to that in the aging chamber at dilute conditions. An unfortunate side effect was that approximately half the smoke was lost from the system because it diffused o

ging process was accelerated compared to that in the aging chamber at dilute conditions. An unfortunate side effect was that approximately half the smoke was lost from the system because it diffused out of the inlet into the MSG volume. As a result the total particle counts were lower than normal and the TEM grids had few particles. It is important to recognize that this condition is unique to low-gravity scenarios. If one performed the same experiment at 1-g, the buoyancy of the rising gases would greatly increase the mixing zone. So the larger particle diameters observed in these zero-flow conditions are important to consider in the development of improved fire detection equipment for space vehicles. For the zero-flow case, the heat is transported primarily by conduction rather than convection. This is likely to result in a significant increase in the gas temperature relative to the case with 8 cm/s air flow. A striking effect of this temperature change is the change in the morphology of the Pyrell smoke from fractal-like clusters with up to 30 primary spheres for the case with a flow of 8 cm/s to spherical particles for the zero-flow condition (Fig 13). The results from the SAME experiment indicate that substantial differences in the size distributions of the smoke particles are evident for the five spacecraft materials that were tested. For the conditions of the SAME experiment, all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are readily detected using an ionization smoke detector. However, the aging results suggest that some materials such as silicone rubber can produce smoke that can reach sizes better detected by light scattering techniques. The zero flow conditions produced smoke particles that were 2 to 3 times larger than those produced at the nominal 8 cm/s flow rate. Since spacecraft fire conditions include an even wider array of materials than those tested here and a broader range of flow and temperature conditions, broad smoke aerosol size distributions can be expected from credible pre-fire overheat events. These results suggest that detection methods that can measure more than one moment of the size distribution may show more successful detection and false alarm rejection than single moment detectors. The results from the prototype 2-moment detector (MPASS) were very encouraging in this respect

The results from the prototype 2-moment detector (MPASS) were very encouraging in this respect with the technique showing real potential as a means to respond to a broad particle range while avoiding excessive false alarms from nuisance sources. The TEM result demonstrated that fire particulate can be expected to have a broad range of morphologies influenced by heating rate, material and flow conditions. IV. ii Smoke Point in Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) Abstract The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the luminous flame length) where a flame begins to emit soot. Smoke points indicate the sooting propensity of a fuel in diffusion flames. In normal gravity, laminar smoke points have been measured for many gaseous and condensed fuels. Laminar smoke points have been found to correlate with soot volume fractions and radiative loss fractions of turbulent diffusion flames. SPICE project measured laminar smoke points in non- buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames in co-flowing air aboard the International Space Station. Fifty-two smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures. Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s. These flames afford extensive control over residence time via variations in dilution, burner diameter, and co-flow velocity. Increasing co-flow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co-flowing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by con

, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co-flowing flames. These trends can be explained qualitatively by considering total residence time effects. The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases. The measured smoke point lengths were found to correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power. The measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity. A model of residence times in coflowing flames is developed, and although residence time helps explain many of the observations, it does not correlate the measured smoke points. The measurements yielded estimates of sooting propensities of the present fuels in microgravity diffusion flames. Acknowledgments The authors acknowledge G.M. Faeth of the University of Michigan for his proposal titled as Laminar Smoke Point Properties of Nonbuoyant Round-Jet Diffusion Flames in response to NASA’s 1996 Solicitation for Glovebox Investigations issued in late 1996. The original proposal of Professor Faeth was meant to be a supplement to the Laminar Soot Processes Experiment which was a combustion project under NASA Grant No. NAG3-1245, conducted onboard STS-73 and STS-94 in 1997. In the awarding letter, the experiment was planned to be carried out onboard STS-107, for which the launch date was then scheduled in May 2000. What Follows is the science significance and justification of the SPICE project. Soot formation in hydrocarbon-fueled flames is an important unresolved problem in combustion science. Soot is estimated to be responsible for up to 52,000 premature deaths annually in the U.S.1 and is believed to contribute to climate change and glacial melting.2 Radiation from soot in flames is beneficial in many applications but also contributes to unwanted heat loads in engines and the spread of fires. Carbon monoxide emitted by smoking flames is the major cause of death in fires.3 Knowledge

2 The differences between soot processes in buoyant and nonbuoyant laminar jet diffusion flames can be seen by comparing their soot production regions as plotted in Fig. 1. Soot formation in diffusion flames generally is limited to fuel-equivalence ratios, φ, in the range 1-2, which are marked on the plots. Unlike gases, which both convect and diffuse, soot mainly convects with the flow velocity so that it moves along the streamline. For buoyant flames, the dividing streamline generally is inside the soot formation region so that most of the soot initially forms near the flame sheet, where φ, =1, and then moves radially inward toward cooler regions having higher fuel concentrations. The soot formation process for nonbuoyant flames is completely different: most of the soot initially forms near the cool core of the flame, where φ is close to 2, and is drawn directly toward the flame sheet. Results from an MSL-1 combustion project, the Laminar Soot Processes (LSP), revealed that the smoke height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in normal gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to be dominated by

height phenomenon in microgravity can be substantially different form that seen in normal gravity. The removal of buoyancy induced acceleration can cause the smoke point phenomenon to be dominated by radiative heat losses for conditions of low overall flame velocity. Under these conditions the flame extinguishes at the flame tip allowing soot to be emitted. In spite of this effect, it is still possible to have flames that either emit soot along all stream lines or do not emit soot anywhere, for conditions where radiation losses do not dominate. Soot path lines through buoyant and non-buoyant flames The information of smoke-point properties and flame shapes is needed to improve our understanding of heat and mass transfer mechanisms for different flame conditions. Unfortunately, while the laminar smoke-point properties of buoyant jet diffusion flames at normal gravity are well known, corresponding information for nonbuoyant flames is limited and questionable. Thus the insights of soot generation and oxidation processes under microgravity conditions are critical to devise better fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploratio

of soot generation and oxidation processes under microgravity conditions are critical to devise better fire safety strategy in spacecraft needed for long term space travels and other space exploration activities. In addition, the improved understanding of soot processes in laminar flames will help us, by analogy, to gain better understanding of soot processes in practical turbulent flames. The objectives of the SPICE experiments is to find the laminar smoke-point properties of non- buoyant jet diffusion flames for several fuels under different nozzle diameter/co-flow velocity configurations. Luminous flame shape measurements would also be made to verify models of the

3 flame shapes under co-flow conditions. In particular, the experiments are planned to be conducted under the following conditions: six types of fuels: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, 75% propylene mixed with 25% nitrogen in moles, and 50% propylene mixed with 50% nitrogen in moles; three nozzles: 0.4, 0.8 and 1.6 mm ID and two air velocities: 100% and 50% of the maximum air flow velocity (near 50cm/s). The operation procedures are as such that the air velocity is set first, then start the fuel flow and ignite the flame. Fuel flow rate is adjusted until the smoke point is reached. Thus, for each combination of a fuel and a nozzle size, two smoke point fuel flow rates are obtained. One is under 100% air velocity and the other is under 50% air velocity. Then in the case of 50% air velocity, the fuel flow rate is reduced to 50% of the smoke point fuel flow rate to get a flame length with that fuel flow rate. SPICE EXPERIMENT SETUP A. 17 DISCUSSION Although it is convenient to classified all flames, laminar vs. turbulent and diffusion vs. premixed, into two categories based on their soot emission conditions, i.e., soot emitting flames and non-soot emitting flames, the conditions delineating the two or the conditions of onset of soot emission are difficult to define. Up to date, these conditions have been documented solely based on experimental observations. Many efforts have been made to develop a universal method of defining the onset of soot emission, i.e., smoke point, conditions, in terms of primary parameters of the flame. But none of these efforts has been quite successful yet. The primary parameters of the flame mentioned here refer to parameters used to set the flame, not those generated by the flame. The primary parameters of jet diffusion flames include fuel type, fuel and oxidizer supply rates, ambient temperature and pressure, and configuration of the device where the flame takes place, such as nozzle diameter and dimensions of the combustion chamber. The flame temperature, gas velocity and species distributions as well as flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat generation and heat loss, are

ameter and dimensions of the combustion chamber. The flame temperature, gas velocity and species distributions as well as flame shapes and derived parameters such as heat generation and heat loss, are the parameters generated by the flame which is not considered as primary parameters. If a method that relates smoke point to those primary parameters were found, we would be able to predict whether a flame emits soot or not based on the planned flame conditions. In the course of pursuing such a universal method, a number of surmises of the mechanism of soot emission have been proposed to associate smoke point with certain flame generated parameters. Those surmises served as a middle step in hoping to help further development of the aforementioned method. The first surmise, and least controversial, is that smoke points occur when soot temperature drops below a critical temperature prior to soot burnout. This temperature is about 1300 K in normal gravity8,9 and 1000 K in microgravity.10,11 The second is that smoke point occurs when radiative loss fraction reaches 0.2 – 0.4 for normal-gravity flames12-16 or 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames.17 Since the radiative fraction of heat loss in

The second is that smoke point occurs when radiative loss fraction reaches 0.2 – 0.4 for normal-gravity flames12-16 or 0.4 – 0.6 for microgravity flames.17 Since the radiative fraction of heat loss increases with fuel flow rate, smoke point will occur as the fuel flow rate is higher than Figure 19. 18 certain value. This is consistent with experimental observations. The third surmise is that the smoke point correlates to the ratio of luminous length divided by stoichiometric length. This ratio increases with flow rate. Once it reaches about 2, smoke point occurs.15,18,19 The last surmise suggests that smoke point correlates with the centerline flame residence time. This is the most complex8-11,17,18,20- 24 surmise because flame residence time affects the soot processes in twofold. An increase in residence time can lead to soot emissions by increasing the time available for soot formation. Because this generally also increases the time available for soot oxidation, it has been proposed that smoke points are associated with conditions where the time available for soot formation exceeds that for soot oxidation to certain extent.21 This is difficult to prove because to evaluate the flame residence time requires the velocity distribution alone the centerline and the flame length, both of which are resulted flame parameters, not readily available from primary parameters of the experiment. In addition, the soot formation time and oxidation time are conceptually defined. Practically,

Practically, these times are not measurable and they might be overlapped, i.e., for the same soot aggregate, adding and oxidizing carbon particles may happen simultaneously. Because of these difficulties and ambiguities, the fame residence time theory cannot be proved or disproved rigorously. The results showed that although residence time is helpful in understanding the present smoke points, it does not yield quantitative correlations. studies.name: BASS
studies.text: BASS (PSI-26): Burning and Suppression of Solids. Flown in space (about 0 g). Tests from 2012 to 2013. 122 tests in the PSI table. Table lists samples only (no airflow, oxygen or results). Use the reports. Materials: PMMA, Wax candle, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass), Nomex.

studies.name: BASS-II
studies.text: BASS-II (PSI-25): Burning and Suppression of Solids - II. Flown in space (about 0 g). Tests from 2014 to 2018. 129 tests in the PSI table. Oxygen: 13.6 to 22.2 %. Materials: PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass), Nomex, Wax candle.

studies.name: SPICE
studies.text: SPICE (PSI-107): Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment. Flown in space (about 0 g). 435 tests in the PSI table. Airflow: 0.7 to 85.3 cm/s. Fuels: 75% Propylene, Propylene, 50% Propylene, Propane, Ethylene, Methane.

studies.name: SLICE
studies.text: SLICE (PSI-106): Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment. Flown in space (about 0 g). Tests in 2012. 12 tests in the PSI table. Table lists test dates and fuels only. Use the reports. Fuels: 100% CH4, 70% CH4 (balance N2), 40% CH4 (balance N2), 20% C2H4 (balance N2), 100% C2H6, 100% C2H4.

studies.name: FLEX
studies.text: FLEX (PSI-69): Flame Extinguishment Experiment. Flown in space (about 0 g). Tests from 2009 to 2011. 274 tests in the PSI table. Oxygen: 12 to 34 %. Pressure: 0.69 to 3.05 atm. Fuels: Methanol, Heptane.

studies.name: FLEX-2
studies.text: FLEX-2 (PSI-68): Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2. Flown in space (about 0 g). No test results in a PSI table. Table is the planned test matrix, not results.

studies.name: CFI
studies.text: CFI (PSI-39): Cool Flames Investigation. Flown in space (about 0 g). Tests in 2017. 87 tests in the PSI table. Oxygen: 17 to 21 %. Pressure: 0.5 to 5 atm. Fuels: 60/40 n-dodecane/iso-dodecane, 75/25 n-dodecane/iso-dodecane, n-dodecane.

studies.name: ACME BRE
studies.text: ACME BRE (PSI-20): Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator. Flown in space (about 0 g). Tests from 2019 to 2021. 18 tests in the PSI table. Oxygen: 21 to 40 %. Fuels: 100% C2H4, 50% C2H4, 100% CH4.

studies.name: ACME CLD Flame
studies.text: ACME CLD Flame (PSI-21): Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame. Flown in space (about 0 g). Tests from 2017 to 2021. 32 tests in the PSI table. Fuels: 40% CH4, 100% C2H4, 50% C2H4, 100% CH4, 30% C2H4.

studies.name: ACME E-FIELD Flames
studies.text: ACME E-FIELD Flames (PSI-22): Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames. Flown in space (about 0 g). Tests in 2018. 32 tests in the PSI table. Fuels: 100% C2H4, 100% CH4, 40% CH4, 30% C2H4.

studies.name: ACME s-Flame
studies.text: ACME s-Flame (PSI-23): Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames. Flown in space (about 0 g). Tests from 2019 to 2020. 18 tests in the PSI table. Oxygen: 21 to 30 %. Pressure: 1 atm. Fuels: 50% C2H4 with N2, 45% CH4 with N2, 100% H2, 44.4% H2 with CH4, 66.7% H2 with CH4, 25% H2, 20% CH4, with He, 20% H2, 25% CH4, with He, 30% H2, 15% CH4, with He, 45% H2 with He, 45% CH4 with He, 20% C2H4 with He, 25% C2H4 with He.

studies.name: ACME Flame Design
studies.text: ACME Flame Design (PSI-10): Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design. Flown in space (about 0 g). 327 tests in the PSI table. Oxygen in the air around normal flames: 19.8 to 40 %. Inside-out (inverse) flames: 21.2 to 85 % oxygen, flowing out of the burner, so not the surrounding air. Pressure: 0.43 to 3.02 atm. Fuels: C2H4, C2H4 (fuel side, inverse flame), C3H8.

studies.name: ACME CFI-G
studies.text: ACME CFI-G (PSI-159): Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases. Flown in space (about 0 g). 179 tests in the PSI table. Oxygen: 18 to 40 %. Pressure: 0.5 to 3 atm. Fuels: 30% butane, 30% propane, 50% butane, 30% ethane, propane, ethane.

studies.name: Saffire-I
studies.text: Saffire-I (PSI-98): Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment-I. Flown in space (about 0 g). 2 tests in the PSI table. Oxygen: 21.5 to 21.7 %. Airflow: 20 cm/s. Materials: SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass). The test table and a NASA source disagree here. Burn time: table says 420 s for sample S1; NASA's 2018 Saffire talk (NTRS 20180005168) says 400 s.

studies.name: Saffire-II
studies.text: Saffire-II (PSI-99): Spacecraft Fire Experiment-II. Flown in space (about 0 g). 7 tests in the PSI table. Oxygen: 21.5 to 22.1 %. Airflow: 20 cm/s. Materials: Silicone, PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass).

studies.name: Saffire-III
studies.text: Saffire-III (PSI-100): Spacecraft Fire Experiment-III. Flown in space (about 0 g). 2 tests in the PSI table. Table has 2 rows. Airflow: 30 cm/s. Materials: SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass). The test table and a NASA source disagree here. Airflow: table says 30 cm/s; NASA's 2018 Saffire talk (NTRS 20180005168) says 25 cm/s.

studies.name: SAME
studies.text: SAME (PSI-102): Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment. Flown in space (about 0 g). 20 tests in the PSI table. Table has 8 rows; samples 5 to 8 reuse the conditions of samples 1 to 4. Airflow: 5 to 10 cm/s. Materials heated to make smoke, not burned (the SAME-2 paper, NTRS 20130000422, says below the ignition point): Teflon, Kapton, Silicone Rubber, Lampwick, Dibutyl Phthalate.

studies.name: SAME-R
studies.text: SAME-R (PSI-101): Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight. Flown in space (about 0 g). 109 tests in the PSI table. Airflow: 0 to 8.1 cm/s. Materials heated to make smoke, not burned (the SAME-2 paper, NTRS 20130000422, says below the ignition point): Kapton, Silicone, Lampwick, Pyrell, Teflon.

studies.name: DAFT
studies.text: DAFT (PSI-47): Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2. Flown in space (about 0 g). Tests in 2005. 2 tests in the PSI table. Table lists 2 test sessions only. Materials: Arizona Road Dust (ARD Fine).

studies.name: PSI-60
studies.text: PSI-60: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets. A ground-based study (1 g), not flown in space. No test results in a PSI table.

studies.name: PSI-62
studies.text: PSI-62: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography. A ground-based study (1 g), not flown in space. No test results in a PSI table.

studies.name: PSI-115
studies.text: PSI-115: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity. A ground-based study (1 g), not flown in space. No test results in a PSI table.

studies.name: PSI-117
studies.text: PSI-117: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis. A ground-based study (1 g), not flown in space. No test results in a PSI table.

studies.name: PSI-142
studies.text: PSI-142: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames. A ground-based study (1 g), not flown in space. No test results in a PSI table.
